summary: Specifies conventions for how S/MIME version 4.0 agents use X.509 certificates. Certificates are central to S/MIME processing, and agents validate them as described in RFC 5280. It is a standards-track document that goes with the S/MIME 4.0 message specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Secure email needs a kind of digital ID card to prove who you are. This document sets the rules for how email programs check and use those ID cards.

questions: which signature algorithms must s/mime support
how does s/mime check the sender email address
subtitle: The certificate rules an email program must follow before it trusts a key for S/MIME signing and encryption.

tldr.problem: Secure email only works if a program can tell that a public key really belongs to the person it claims to. S/MIME needs a common set of certificate rules so different mail programs agree.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME agents must validate X.509 certificates as RFC 5280 describes, plus extra rules here: how email addresses appear in certificates, which signature algorithms and key sizes to support, and how key usage extensions are read.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5750 (S/MIME 3.2 certificate handling) and requires ECDSA with P-256 and EdDSA with curve25519, while pushing RSA keys under 2048 bits and the old SHA-1 and MD5 algorithms out of use.

facts.label: Required signature algorithms
facts.value: ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256; EdDSA with curve25519

today: RFC 8550 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2019. It obsoletes RFC 5750 and is meant to be used with the S/MIME 4.0 message specification in RFC 8551. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why S/MIME Needs Certificate Rules
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) version 4.0, described in RFC 8551, sends and receives secure MIME messages. Before an S/MIME agent uses a public key for any security service, it MUST verify that the key is valid. To do that it MUST use PKIX certificates as described in RFC 5280, and it MUST also meet the extra requirements in this document.

An S/MIME agent is user software that is a sending agent, a receiving agent, or both. The specification uses the data types of the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and inherits the certificate-based key management architectures that CMS supports.

The document also defines three extra requirement levels: SHOULD+ (expected to become a MUST later), SHOULD- (expected to become a MAY) and MUST- (expected to stop being a MUST, but to stay at least a SHOULD-).
sections.plainLanguage: Before you trust a note that says it is from your friend, you want proof. A certificate is that proof, and this document says exactly how mail programs must check it.

sections.title: CMS Options: CRLs, Certificate Types and Included Certificates
sections.content:
Receiving agents MUST support the CRL format in RFC 5280, both version 1 and version 2, and MUST recognize CRLs in received messages. A certificate revocation list (CRL) names certificates their issuer has revoked. Agents SHOULD store CRLs they receive for later messages.

Receiving agents MUST support version 1 and version 3 X.509 certificates, and SHOULD support version 2 attribute certificates. Sending and receiving agents MUST NOT use PKCS #6 extended certificates, though receivers must be able to parse a message that contains them (ignoring them is expected). Sending agents MUST NOT send version 1 attribute certificates.

Receiving agents MUST handle any number of included certificates in any order. Sending agents SHOULD include the sender's certificates and issuer certificates, including at least one chain up to, but not including, a CA the recipient may trust. Receivers SHOULD NOT simply trust self-signed certificates as valid CAs, and MUST support chaining based on distinguished name fields.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a signed letter, you should also tuck in the ID card and the papers that vouch for it. The reader must cope with any pile of papers, in any order.

sections.title: Email Addresses in Certificates
sections.content:
End-entity certificates MAY contain an Internet mail address. The address SHOULD be in the subjectAltName extension and SHOULD NOT be in the subject distinguished name. ASCII addresses use the rfc822Name form from RFC 5280; internationalized addresses use the encoding defined in RFC 8398, and support for them is required.

Receiving agents MUST accept certificates that contain no email address, and MUST recognize addresses in the PKCS #9 emailAddress attribute of the distinguished name, which is an IA5String with an upper bound of 255 characters.

For ASCII addresses, the domain part (right of the @) MUST be compared case-insensitively, and the local part SHOULD be. If the certificate has addresses, a receiving agent MUST check that the address in the From or Sender header matches one of them, and SHOULD provide some explicit alternate processing if it does not, such as showing the addresses in the certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID card should have your email address on it, and the mail program checks that the sender's address matches the card. If not, it should warn you.

sections.title: Finding and Validating Certificates
sections.content:
Agents need some way to retrieve certificates for recipients. The RFC mentions an X.500 directory and an experimental DNS-based scheme (RFC 8162), and notes that at a minimum an agent could generate a message asking the recipient to reply with a signed message. Agents SHOULD let users store and protect correspondents' certificates, like an address book, and SHOULD support import and export using a CMS certs-only message.

Certificate, CRL and path validation MUST be performed as per RFC 5280 before a public key is used to verify a signature or to encrypt or derive a key. Certificates and CRLs from incoming messages SHOULD be cached to help path validation. Agents SHOULD retrieve and use CRL information every time a certificate is verified, although the RFC admits that offline verification may make the latest CRL hard to get.

To find the signer's certificate, an agent SHALL use a signingCertificate or signingCertificateV2 attribute if present. Otherwise it uses issuerAndSerialNumber or subjectKeyIdentifier.
sections.plainLanguage: You need a way to look up other people's ID cards and a safe place to keep them. Every time you check one, you also look at the list of cards that have been cancelled.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms and Key Sizes
sections.content:
Certificates and CRLs are signed by their issuer. Receiving agents MUST support ECDSA with curve P-256 with SHA-256 and EdDSA with curve25519 in PureEdDSA mode. They MUST- support RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 with SHA-256, and SHOULD support RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256. Implementations SHOULD use deterministic generation of the ECDSA parameter k (RFC 6979).

RSA and RSASSA-PSS key sizes for verifying certificate and CRL signatures are graded: key sizes up to 2047 bits are SHOULD NOT, 2048 to 4096 bits are MUST, and above 4096 bits are MAY. Curves other than P-256 and curve25519 MAY also be used.

Appendix A explains that RSA with MD5, RSA and DSA with SHA-1, and DSA with SHA-256 were dropped in S/MIME 4.0, because MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer collision resistant and DSA was replaced by elliptic curve versions. Support for these may still be needed for historic messages, but they SHOULD NOT be used for new artifacts.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature on an ID card is like a stamp. This section says which stamps are strong enough today and which old stamps are too easy to fake.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
Agents MUST correctly handle the basic constraints, key usage, authority key identifier, subject key identifier and subject alternative name extensions. S/MIME certificates SHOULD NOT contain critical extensions other than those listed, and extensions SHOULD be marked non-critical unless correct handling is essential to interpreting the certificate.

  • Basic constraints MUST be in CA certificates and SHOULD NOT be in end-entity certificates.
  • Key usage, if present, MUST be marked critical. A signature MUST NOT be accepted if the certificate has a key usage extension without at least one of the digitalSignature or nonRepudiation bits. If the extension is absent, receivers MUST presume both bits are set.
  • Subject alternative name is the preferred place for email addresses, and multiple addresses MAY be present.
  • Extended key usage, if present, must contain id-kp-emailProtection or anyExtendedKeyUsage for interpersonal-message agents. The permitted uses are the intersection of key usage and extended key usage.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions are extra notes on the ID card, such as what the card may be used for. If a note says the card is only for signing, you cannot use it for locking messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a certificate is not provably valid and associated with the message, the software should take immediate and noticeable steps to tell the user. Failure cases include no matching email address, no chain to a trusted CA, no ability to check the CRL, an invalid or expired CRL, an expired certificate and a revoked certificate.

A sender could deliberately include an older unexpired CRL that lacks a recent revocation, so agents SHOULD consult the most recently issued CRL for the CA. Validity checks should use a reliable time, normally the current time. A signingTime attribute could be set deliberately to a time that makes a revoked or expired certificate look fine.

Certificates not yet validated to a trust anchor can be manufactured to mount denial-of-service attacks, for example with keys that need excessive processing or long lists of CRL Distribution Point and Authority Information Access addresses. RSA keys under 2048 bits are considered by many experts to be insecure; an implementation that verifies RSA or DSA keys under 2048 bits MUST warn the user, and servers where warnings are not appropriate SHOULD reject messages with weak cryptography.
sections.plainLanguage: A cheater might show you an old list or a fake card. So the program should always use the newest list, trust a reliable clock, and shout a warning when something looks wrong.

sections.title: Version History and Compatibility
sections.content:
S/MIME 4.0 agents ought to be as interoperable as possible with earlier versions: version 2 is described in RFC 2311 through RFC 2315, version 3 in RFC 2630 through RFC 2634 and RFC 5035, version 3.1 in RFC 2634, RFC 3850, RFC 3851, RFC 3852 and RFC 5035, and version 3.2 in RFC 2634, RFC 5035, RFC 5652, RFC 5750 and RFC 5751.

The document lists changes at each step. Version 3.1 required support for version 1 and 2 CRLs and overlapping CA certificates. Version 3.2 added RSA with SHA-256 as a MUST and aligned with PKIX. Version 4.0 required internationalized email addresses, mandated ECDSA and EdDSA, treated SHA-1, MD5 and DSA as historical and raised lower bounds on RSA key sizes. Appendix B notes that S/MIME v2 certificate handling (RFC 2312) was moved to Historic status.
sections.plainLanguage: Email security has had several versions, like game updates. This one tells you what changed each time and keeps old messages readable.
